John Searle

John Searle (1932–) attacked the computational theory of mind with the Chinese Room thought experiment 1: a person who follows rules to manipulate Chinese characters can produce correct outputs without understanding a word of Chinese. Syntax (computation) is not sufficient for semantics (meaning). His alternative, biological naturalism, holds that consciousness is a real, causally efficacious biological phenomenon produced by specific neurobiological processes—not by the abstract formal structure that any computer might share with a brain.

Daniel Dennett

Daniel Dennett (1942–2024) rejected the Cartesian theater—the assumption that there is a single place in the brain where “it all comes together” for a conscious observer 2. Instead, he proposed the Multiple Drafts model: at any moment, multiple parallel streams of content are being revised and edited throughout the brain, and there is no sharp line between conscious and unconscious processing. His intentional stance 3 treats the attribution of beliefs and desires as a predictive strategy: we model systems as if they have beliefs and goals because doing so lets us predict their behavior, regardless of their internal architecture.

Patricia Churchland

Patricia Churchland (1943–) coined neurophilosophy and argued that traditional philosophical categories—belief, desire, intention—may not carve the brain at its joints 4. As neuroscience matures, these folk-psychological concepts may be revised or eliminated entirely in favor of neuroscientific categories (eliminative materialism). Philosophy of mind, on this view, must be continuous with and constrained by brain science. Her work has been instrumental in breaking down disciplinary barriers between philosophy and neuroscience.

David Chalmers

David Chalmers (1966–) drew the sharpest contemporary distinction between what a computational theory of the brain can and cannot explain 5, 6. The easy problems—explaining discrimination, integration, reportability, attentional control—are hard in practice but easy in principle: they are functional problems amenable to computational explanation. The hard problem is why and how any of this functional processing is accompanied by subjective experience (qualia). A perfect Bayesian world model running in a brain would solve all the easy problems; whether it would thereby solve the hard problem remains the deepest open question in the field.

Francisco Varela

Francisco Varela (1946–2001), with Humberto Maturana, introduced autopoiesis: a living system is a self-producing network of processes that generates and maintains its own boundary 7. With Evan Thompson and Eleanor Rosch, he then developed enactivism: cognition is not the construction of a representation of a pre-given world but the enactment of a world through the organism’s embodied activity 8. His program of neurophenomenology 9 called for first-person phenomenological reports to be used as data constraining third-person neuroscientific models—a bridge between the manifest and scientific images.

Paul Churchland

Paul Churchland (1942–) argued that cognition is best understood not as logical inference over sentence-like representations but as the learned transformation of high-dimensional activation patterns across neural populations 10, 11. His state-space semantics proposes that a concept is not a symbol but a region in a high-dimensional neural activation space, and that semantic similarity is geometric proximity in that space. Learning is the sculpting of synaptic weights so that the network’s activation landscape comes to mirror the statistical structure of the environment—a view that harmonizes with both modern deep learning and with the predictive processing claim that the brain’s generative model is a learned mapping from hidden causes to expected sensory states. If Patricia Churchland argued that philosophy must become neuroscience, Paul Churchland showed what a neurocomputational philosophy of mind might look like in practice.

Alva Noë (1964–) developed a radically anti-representationalist enactivism 12, 13. Perception, he argued, is not something that happens inside the brain; it is something the whole organism does—a skillful, exploratory activity governed by the perceiver’s implicit mastery of sensorimotor contingencies: the lawful ways in which sensory stimulation changes as a function of the organism’s own movement. We do not need a rich internal world model, on this view, because the world is perpetually available to be sampled through action; the brain’s role is not to build a detailed internal replica but to facilitate ongoing, dynamic access to environmental structure. Noë’s enactivism poses the sharpest form of the question that every predictive processing theorist must answer: if the brain is a prediction machine that models the world, does it genuinely represent the world, or does it merely anticipate the sensory consequences of its own actions—and is there, in the end, a difference?
